analysis.one_liner: Reinstates taxes on oil and chemical companies to fund toxic waste site cleanups.
analysis.headline: The bill would have made oil and chemical companies pay to clean up toxic waste sites, but it never got a vote in the Senate Finance Committee before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill brings back the "polluter pays" taxes that once funded the Superfund, the government program that cleans up the nation's worst toxic waste sites. Oil companies would pay 17.2 cents per barrel of crude oil (up from 9.7 cents before the tax lapsed in 1995), chemical manufacturers would pay per-ton fees on 42 listed chemicals, and both rates would rise with inflation. It also covers oil from tar sands and oil shale, and lets the cleanup fund be spent without a separate vote by Congress each year.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near the roughly 1,300 contaminated sites on the Superfund list, and taxpayers generally, benefit: cleanup money would come from the oil and chemical companies whose products created the waste instead of from ordinary income-tax payers, and the fund could be spent without waiting on annual congressional appropriations. The tax lapsed in 1995, and since then general taxpayer money has carried most of the cleanup burden.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents near toxic sites and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Restores the dedicated tax on crude oil and petroleum products — raised from 9.7 to 17.2 cents per barrel and indexed to inflation — so the companies that profit from oil fund the cleanup of hazardous waste.

Reinstates per-ton excise taxes on 42 hazardous chemicals, from benzene and mercury to sulfuric acid, with rates adjusted for inflation, reinstating the principle that chemical producers pay into the cleanup fund.
Expands the tax to cover oil derived from tar sands and oil shale, closing a gap that let those producers escape the fee.

Makes the Superfund trust fund available for cleanups 'without further appropriation,' meaning the program no longer has to wait for Congress to pass a spending bill each year before it can clean up sites.

analysis.who_pays: Oil producers, refiners, and importers pay 17.2 cents per barrel (rising with inflation), and chemical manufacturers pay per-ton fees on listed chemicals. Part of those excise taxes would be passed along in the price of fuel and chemical-based goods, though the amounts are small relative to the price of a barrel of oil or a ton of a chemical.

drawbacks.text: Excise taxes on oil and chemicals are partly passed through to consumers in the form of slightly higher prices for gasoline, plastics, and other chemical-based goods, so some of the cost would land on ordinary households even though the tax targets industry.
The bill lets the Superfund trust fund be spent without a separate annual appropriation from Congress, which removes a regular point of congressional oversight over how cleanup money is used.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and long-running: since the polluter-pays taxes expired in 1995, general taxpayers have funded most Superfund cleanups, and this bill shifts that burden back onto the oil and chemical companies whose products generated the waste, while also guaranteeing the fund money without yearly appropriations fights. The cost is modest — fractions of a cent passed through to fuel and chemical prices — and the loss of annual appropriations oversight is a trade-off, not a fatal flaw. A bill that got two cosponsors and no committee action was never seriously weighed against these costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the Superfund Polluter Pays Restoration Act on June 22, 2021, along with Senators Whitehouse and Menendez.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day; no hearing, markup, or vote followed.
It attracted only two cosponsors during its entire life, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 without the bill ever leaving committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and chemical companies are better off: they avoided paying the reinstated excise taxes, and the cost of cleaning the nation's toxic waste sites continued to fall on general taxpayers instead.

sides.party_line_note: Only three Democratic senators sponsored or cosponsored the bill and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of the Senate as a whole was never tested.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: The bill reinstates and roughly doubles the per-barrel Superfund tax to 17.2 cents and extends it to tar sands and oil shale-derived oil. The industry's interest in avoiding the fee runs against the public's interest in having polluters, not taxpayers, fund toxic cleanups.

Per-ton excise taxes on 42 hazardous chemicals, including benzene, mercury, and chlorine, would be reinstated and indexed to inflation. These companies have paid nothing into the fund since the tax lapsed in 1995 while their products remain a major source of Superfund contamination.
